scenarios.title: Bag Weight Label
scenarios.context: A student has one school bag with a weight written on a scale.
scenarios.prompt: What single piece of information would you store so the computer can remember the bag weight?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I only need to remember the bag weight, so I would store it with a clear name.

scenarios.title: Rainy Day Choice
scenarios.context: Before leaving home, a learner checks whether it is raining.
scenarios.prompt: What small decision rule would help the learner decide whether to carry an umbrella?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: If it is raining, carry an umbrella. Otherwise, leave it at home.

scenarios.title: Two Snack Prices
scenarios.context: A learner buys one samosa and one juice from the canteen.
scenarios.prompt: How would you figure out the total cost using just the two prices?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would keep the two prices separately and add them to get the total.

scenarios.title: Greeting by Name
scenarios.context: A classroom screen should greet one learner by name.
scenarios.prompt: What text should the computer remember, and how should it combine that text into a greeting?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: The computer should store the learner name and place it inside a greeting sentence.

scenarios.title: Pass Mark Check
scenarios.context: A learner receives one test score and wants to know whether it is at least the pass mark.
scenarios.prompt: What comparison would decide if the learner passed?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would compare the score with the pass mark and decide pass if it is high enough.

scenarios.title: Pocket Money Left
scenarios.context: A learner starts with pocket money and spends a small amount on stationery.
scenarios.prompt: What two values matter, and how would you find the money left?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Start with the original money, subtract the spent amount, and store what remains.

scenarios.title: Favorite Color List
scenarios.context: Three friends each say their favorite color.
scenarios.prompt: How would you keep all three colors together instead of making separate notes?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Since all values are colors, I would keep them together in one list.

scenarios.title: First Item in a Bag
scenarios.context: A bag contains a pencil, eraser, and ruler in that order.
scenarios.prompt: How would you ask for only the first item?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: The first item is based on its position in the ordered group.

scenarios.title: Attendance Count
scenarios.context: A teacher has a short list of students present today.
scenarios.prompt: What question would help you find how many students are present?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: I would count how many names are in the present-students list.

scenarios.title: Temperature Message
scenarios.context: A weather display has one temperature reading.
scenarios.prompt: What simple rule would decide whether to show Hot or Comfortable?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: If the temperature is above the threshold, show Hot; otherwise show Comfortable.

scenarios.title: Water Bottle Reminder
scenarios.context: A learner wants a reminder for each break in the school day.
scenarios.prompt: How would you avoid writing the same reminder separately for every break?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: For every break, show the same water reminder.

scenarios.title: Find the Longest Pencil
scenarios.context: A learner has several pencil lengths and wants to know which one is longest.
scenarios.prompt: What small comparison would you repeat as you look through the lengths?
objectives: Compare one item at a time
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Start with one pencil as the longest, then compare each next pencil against it.

scenarios.title: Clean Chore Checklist
scenarios.context: A family has a checklist of small chores for Saturday morning.
scenarios.prompt: How would you go through each chore and mark it as done?
objectives: Process one chore at a time
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Put chores in a list and handle each chore one by one.

scenarios.title: Movie Age Filter
scenarios.context: A movie app has a list of films, each with a minimum age.
scenarios.prompt: What rule would decide which movies a 12-year-old can see?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: For each movie, keep it only if the learner age is at least the minimum age.

scenarios.title: Classroom Supply Lookup
scenarios.context: A class monitor tracks how many chalk pieces, markers, and notebooks are available.
scenarios.prompt: How would you store each supply name with its count?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Each supply has a count, so I would store supply names as keys with counts as values.

scenarios.title: Bus Stop Search
scenarios.context: A route list contains several bus stops, and a learner wants to know if Library Stop is included.
scenarios.prompt: How would you check the stops one at a time until you find the target?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Look at each stop and compare it with the stop I want.

scenarios.title: Average Practice Score
scenarios.context: A learner has five practice scores and wants one average score.
scenarios.prompt: What two small steps are needed before dividing?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Find the total of all scores, count how many scores there are, then divide.

scenarios.title: Separate Even Roll Numbers
scenarios.context: A class list has roll numbers, and the teacher wants only even-numbered students for Team A.
scenarios.prompt: What small test tells you whether a roll number is even?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: A roll number is even if dividing by two leaves no remainder.

scenarios.title: Capitalize Name Tags
scenarios.context: A club has names typed in lowercase and wants neat name tags.
scenarios.prompt: What same text-cleaning action should happen to every name?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: For each name, convert it to title case before printing the tag.

scenarios.title: Find Missing Homework
scenarios.context: A teacher has one list of all students and another list of students who submitted homework.
scenarios.prompt: How would you reason about who is missing from the submitted list?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Take everyone in the class and remove the students who submitted.

scenarios.title: Reusable Discount Rule
scenarios.context: A shop gives the same discount rule to many different bills.
scenarios.prompt: What inputs should a reusable discount helper receive?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: The helper needs the bill amount and should return the final price after applying the rule.

scenarios.title: Mini Quiz Checker
scenarios.context: A quiz app needs to check one answer against one correct answer.
scenarios.prompt: How would you design a tiny reusable checker for one question?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Compare the learner answer with the correct answer and return whether they match.

scenarios.title: Step Counter Function
scenarios.context: A fitness note has a list of step counts from different walks.
scenarios.prompt: How would you make a reusable helper that returns the total steps?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: The function should take step counts, add them, and give back the total.

scenarios.title: Safe Username Maker
scenarios.context: A classroom app needs to turn a full name into a simple username.
scenarios.prompt: What small text transformations should a username function perform?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Make the name lowercase and remove spaces so it can be used as a username.

scenarios.title: Retry Until Valid
scenarios.context: A form should keep asking until the learner enters a positive number.
scenarios.prompt: What condition tells the program to keep asking?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Keep asking while the number is not positive, then stop once it is valid.

scenarios.title: Simple Score Report
scenarios.context: A tutor wants a small report showing a learner name and score together.
scenarios.prompt: How would you package two related pieces of information in one result?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Return a dictionary with the learner name and score as labeled values.

scenarios.title: Task Status Updater
scenarios.context: A to-do app has tasks with statuses and needs to mark one task as done.
scenarios.prompt: What exact value changes when a task is completed?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Find the task by name and change its status from pending to done.

scenarios.title: Small Receipt Builder
scenarios.context: A cafe wants a short text receipt for one item and its price.
scenarios.prompt: What pieces should a receipt function combine into a readable line?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Combine the item name and price into one clear sentence.

scenarios.title: Choose Next Scenario
scenarios.context: PyBe wants to choose an easier or harder next scenario based on one score.
scenarios.prompt: What simple score rule could decide the next difficulty?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: If the score is high choose harder, if low choose easier, otherwise stay similar.

scenarios.title: Reflection Keyword Finder
scenarios.context: PyBe reads a short reflection and checks whether the learner mentioned confusion.
scenarios.prompt: What tiny search would detect that the reflection may need extra support?
scenarios.sampleReasoning: Look for words like confused or stuck and flag the reflection if they appear.

variables.title: Variables

w3h.what: A variable is a named container that stores a value you can use later. Think of it as a labeled box where you put information to retrieve whenever needed.
w3h.why: Programs need to remember values—user input, calculations, game scores. Without variables, every piece of data would be lost after use.
w3h.how: Assign a value using the = sign. The name goes on the left, the value on the right. You can then use the name to retrieve or change that value later.

variables.commonMistake: Using a variable name that hasn't been assigned yet, or trying to use a variable before giving it a value.
variables.keyTakeaway: Variables let programs store, name, and reuse information.

conditionals.title: Conditionals

w3h.what: Conditionals are decisions in code. They let programs choose different actions based on whether something is true or false.
w3h.why: Real life is full of choices. Conditionals let your program respond differently depending on the situation—should I bring an umbrella? Should I show a pass or fail message?
w3h.how: Use if, elif (else if), and else to create branching paths. The program checks a condition and follows the matching path.

conditionals.keyTakeaway: Conditionals let programs make decisions and take different paths based on values.

loops.title: Loops

w3h.what: Loops repeat actions without having to write the same code multiple times. They let programs automate repetitive tasks efficiently.
w3h.why: Imagine sending reminder emails to 1000 users—writing that code 1000 times would be impossible. Loops solve this by repeating actions automatically.
where: Processing customer orders in a day
Scanning items in a shopping cart
w3h.how: Use 'for' when you know how many times to repeat. Use 'while' when you want to repeat until a condition becomes false.
w3h.example:
for i in range(5):
    print('Reminder', i)

loops.commonMistake: Creating an infinite loop by forgetting to update the condition variable.
loops.keyTakeaway: Loops automate repetition, saving time and reducing code duplication.

lists.title: Lists

w3h.what: A list is an ordered collection of items stored together. Each item has a position (index) that lets you access it.
w3h.why: Sometimes you need to store multiple related values—names of students, prices of items, tasks to complete. Lists keep them organized together.
w3h.how: Create a list using square brackets. Access items by their index starting from 0. Use loops to process each item.

lists.commonMistake: Forgetting that list indices start from 0, not 1.
lists.keyTakeaway: Lists store multiple related values in order, accessible by position.

functions.title: Functions

w3h.what: A function is a reusable block of code that performs a specific task. You can call it by name whenever you need that task done.
w3h.why: Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, functions let you define it once and reuse it. They also organize code into logical blocks.
w3h.how: Define with 'def', give it a name, add parameters for input. Call the function by name and pass arguments if needed.

functions.commonMistake: Forgetting to return a value when the function should produce output.
functions.keyTakeaway: Functions encapsulate reusable logic, making code organized and maintainable.

strings.title: Strings

w3h.what: A string is text—letters, words, or sentences enclosed in quotes. It's how programs handle written information.
w3h.why: Programs communicate with users through text. Strings let you display messages, process user input, and manipulate textual data.
w3h.how: Create strings with single or double quotes. Combine with +. Extract parts using indices. Use methods like .upper() or .lower().

strings.commonMistake: Confusing strings with numbers. '5' + '3' gives '53', not 8.
strings.keyTakeaway: Strings handle text data and can be combined, compared, and transformed.

arithmetic.title: Arithmetic

w3h.what: Arithmetic operations let programs perform mathematical calculations—addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and more.
w3h.why: From calculating shopping totals to measuring distances, programs often need to compute numerical results.
w3h.how: Use +, -, *, / for basic operations. Use // for integer division, % for remainder, ** for exponents.
w3h.example:
price = 50
tax = price * 0.18
total = price + tax

arithmetic.commonMistake: Using / for division which gives decimals, when you need whole numbers.
arithmetic.keyTakeaway: Arithmetic lets programs perform calculations on numbers.

subtraction.title: Subtraction

w3h.what: Subtraction finds the difference between two numbers by taking one away from another.
w3h.why: Used when you need to find what remains after removing something—calculating change, remaining balance, or distance traveled.
w3h.how: Use the - operator. Order matters: a - b is not the same as b - a.

subtraction.commonMistake: Forgetting that subtraction is not commutative—operand order matters.
subtraction.keyTakeaway: Subtraction finds the difference between two values.

comparisons.title: Comparisons

w3h.what: Comparisons check relationships between values—they ask questions like 'is this bigger?' or 'are these equal?' and return true or false.
w3h.why: Programs constantly need to make decisions. Comparisons provide the answers that drive conditional logic.
w3h.how: Use == for equals, != for not equals, > < >= <= for size comparisons. Results are True or False.

comparisons.commonMistake: Using = instead of == in conditions—the first assigns, the second compares.
comparisons.keyTakeaway: Comparisons produce True/False values used in decision-making.

comparison.title: Comparison

w3h.what: Comparison is the act of examining two things to find similarities or differences. In programming, it means checking relationships between values.
w3h.why: To make decisions, programs must compare values—is this item in the list? Is the password correct? Is there enough inventory?
w3h.how: Compare using operators (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) or methods like sorted() that internally compare elements.

comparison.commonMistake: Assuming transitivity without testing: if a < b and b < c, then a < c.
comparison.keyTakeaway: Comparison enables programs to evaluate relationships and make data-driven decisions.

counting.title: Counting

w3h.what: Counting determines how many items are in a collection. It answers 'how many?' questions.
w3h.why: From counting inventory to tallying votes, programs often need to know quantities to make decisions.
w3h.how: Use len() to get the number of items in a list, string, or collection. Use loops with a counter variable.

counting.commonMistake: Counting from 1 in your head while the program counts from 0.
counting.keyTakeaway: Counting quantifies collections, helping programs know 'how many'.

indexing.title: Indexing

w3h.what: Indexing accesses a specific item in an ordered collection using its position number, starting from 0.
w3h.why: Once items are stored together, you need a way to retrieve specific ones—first item, fifth item, last item.
where: Selecting a contact from a list
Choosing a character from a word
w3h.how: Use square brackets with the position number. First item is index 0, second is 1, etc. Use negative indices for counting from the end.

indexing.commonMistake: Assuming indexing starts at 1 instead of 0, causing off-by-one errors.
indexing.keyTakeaway: Indexing locates items by their position in ordered collections.

dictionaries.title: Dictionaries

w3h.what: A dictionary stores data as key-value pairs. Each key uniquely identifies its value, like a real dictionary where words define meanings.
w3h.why: When you need to look up information by name rather than position, dictionaries are perfect. They're faster than lists for searching.
w3h.how: Create with curly braces. Define keys and values separated by colon. Access values using keys in square brackets.

dictionaries.commonMistake: Trying to access a key that doesn't exist without using .get() for safe lookup.
dictionaries.keyTakeaway: Dictionaries store data as key-value pairs for fast lookup by name.

filtering.title: Filtering

w3h.what: Filtering selects only the items that meet certain conditions, keeping what you need and discarding the rest.
w3h.why: From hundreds of emails, you want only unread ones. From many products, only those in your budget. Filtering solves information overload.
w3h.how: Use conditionals inside loops or list comprehensions. Check each item and keep only those where the condition is true.
w3h.example:
scores = [45, 72, 90, 55, 88]
passing = [s for s in scores if s >= 60]
# [72, 90, 88]

filtering.commonMistake: Modifying a list while iterating over it, causing unexpected behavior.
filtering.keyTakeaway: Filtering extracts subset of data meeting specific criteria.

search.title: Search

w3h.what: Search looks for a specific item or pattern within data, checking each element until a match is found.
w3h.why: Finding whether something exists—whether a username is taken, a word is in a document, or a route exists in a map.
w3h.how: Loop through items checking each one. Use 'in' operator for simple checks. Stop when found for efficiency.

search.commonMistake: Not handling the case when the item isn't found.
search.keyTakeaway: Search locates items by checking elements until a match is found.

sets.title: Sets

w3h.what: A set is a collection of unique items with no duplicates. It automatically removes repeated values.
w3h.why: When you need to track what's in a collection without repeats—like unique visitors, available colors, or allowed permissions.
w3h.how: Create with curly braces or set() function. Add items with .add(). Check membership with 'in'. Sets don't preserve order.

sets.commonMistake: Assuming sets maintain insertion order—they don't.
sets.keyTakeaway: Sets store unique items, automatically removing duplicates.

modulo.title: Modulo

w3h.what: The modulo operator (%) returns the remainder after division. It answers 'what's left over?' when dividing.
w3h.why: Useful for checking divisibility (is this even?), cycling through patterns, or wrapping values within a range.
w3h.how: Use the % operator. 10 % 3 = 1 because 10 divided by 3 is 3 with remainder 1.

modulo.commonMistake: Confusing modulo with division—% gives remainder, / gives quotient.
modulo.keyTakeaway: Modulo finds remainders, useful for patterns and divisibility checks.

averages.title: Averages

w3h.what: An average summarizes a set of numbers with one representative value—the sum divided by the count.
w3h.why: A single average makes large datasets understandable. What's the average score? Average temperature? Average spending?
w3h.how: Sum all values with sum(), count with len(), divide to get average. Formula: (sum of items) / (number of items).

averages.commonMistake: Forgetting to convert to float when dividing—may lose decimal precision.
averages.keyTakeaway: Averages summarize collections with a single representative value.

validation.title: Validation

w3h.what: Validation checks whether data meets requirements before accepting it—confirming it's in the right format, range, or type.
w3h.why: Bad input causes crashes and security issues. Validation catches problems early with clear error messages.
w3h.how: Check each requirement with conditionals. Return True if valid, False otherwise. Provide clear error messages.

validation.commonMistake: Validating only at the end rather than checking incrementally.
validation.keyTakeaway: Validation ensures data meets requirements before processing.

mutation.title: Mutation

w3h.what: Mutation changes an existing value in place rather than creating a new one. The variable stays the same but its contents change.
w3h.why: Sometimes you need to update data without creating copies—like changing a task status, updating a score, or modifying a counter.
w3h.how: Assign a new value to an existing variable or list element. Use += for incrementing. Modify dictionaries with assignment.
w3h.example:
tasks = ['buy milk', 'read book']
tasks[0] = 'buy eggs'
# ['buy eggs', 'read book']

mutation.commonMistake: Mutating shared data unexpectedly affecting other parts of the program.
mutation.keyTakeaway: Mutation updates existing data in place, changing values without creating new variables.

formatting.title: Formatting

w3h.what: Formatting arranges text and numbers into a readable presentation—controlling decimals, alignment, and text layout.
w3h.why: Raw numbers aren't readable. $1234.567890 needs to become '$1,234.57' for receipts, invoices, and reports.
w3h.how: Use f-strings with : for formatting. Control decimal places with .2f, add commas with :, align with < ^ >.

formatting.commonMistake: Using formatting only at display time instead of storing formatted values separately.
formatting.keyTakeaway: Formatting arranges data for clear, attractive presentation.

while loops.title: While Loops

w3h.what: A while loop repeats as long as a condition remains true. Unlike for loops, it continues until something changes the condition.
w3h.why: When you don't know in advance how many repetitions are needed—like waiting for valid user input or processing until data runs out.
w3h.how: Start with 'while condition:'. Inside the loop, ensure the condition eventually becomes False, or you'll loop forever.

while loops.commonMistake: Forgetting to update the condition inside the loop, creating an infinite loop.
while loops.keyTakeaway: While loops repeat until a condition becomes false, useful when repetition count is unknown.

adaptive logic.title: Adaptive Logic

w3h.what: Adaptive logic adjusts behavior based on context or history—making programs respond intelligently to changing conditions.
w3h.why: Static programs can't handle variation. Adaptive systems adjust difficulty, personalize experiences, or optimize based on performance.
w3h.how: Track history or context. Use conditions to select different paths. Update tracking variables as conditions change.

adaptive logic.commonMistake: Adding too many adaptation rules, making the logic complex and hard to maintain.
adaptive logic.keyTakeaway: Adaptive logic adjusts program behavior based on context and history.
